nameStory: The American redstart gets its name from the striking orange-red patches on its wings and tail that flash like flames when it moves. The word 'start' comes from an old English word meaning 'tail,' so 'redstart' literally means 'red tail.' It's called 'American' to distinguish it from the completely unrelated Old World redstart found in Europe.
description: The American redstart is a small, energetic warbler about the size of a chickadee. Males are striking black birds with bright orange patches on their wings, tail, and sides that flash like tiny flames when they fly. Females and young males are gray-olive with yellow patches instead of orange. These active little birds are constantly in motion, fanning their tails and drooping their wings as they hunt for insects.

idTips.label: Flashing tail pattern
idTips.description: Watch for the distinctive habit of fanning and flicking the tail constantly, showing off bright orange (males) or yellow (females) patches at the base of the outer tail feathers

idTips.label: Wing patches
idTips.description: Bright orange or yellow patches on the wings that flash conspicuously during flight and when the bird moves through branches

idTips.label: Restless behavior
idTips.description: Never sits still - constantly flicks wings, spreads tail, and moves in quick, jerky motions while foraging, like a hyperactive butterfly

idTips.label: Male coloring
idTips.description: Adult males are jet black above and on the throat with brilliant orange-red patches on wings, tail, and sides - unmistakable when seen clearly

idTips.label: Female coloring
idTips.description: Females and young males are gray-brown above with white underparts and yellow patches where males have orange

idTips.label: Drooped wing display
idTips.description: Often holds wings slightly drooped and away from the body, showing off the colorful wing patches even when perched

habitat: Look for American redstarts in young deciduous and mixed forests, especially areas with dense understory growth. They love forest edges, second-growth woodlands, and areas recovering from logging or natural disturbances. During migration, you'll also find them in parks, gardens, and wooded suburban areas with plenty of shrubs and small trees.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in May during peak warbler migration. Males are in full breeding plumage with brilliant orange patches and can be heard singing their distinctive high, thin song from treetops.
seasonality.summer: Actively nesting and feeding young. Both parents are constantly foraging, making them easier to spot as they hunt insects in the lower canopy and understory.
seasonality.fall: Present through September during fall migration. Many birds are in duller plumage, with young males looking similar to females, but the tail-flashing behavior remains constant.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - these birds migrate to Central America and northern South America where insects remain abundant year-round.

funFact: American redstarts are like tiny feathered matadors, using their colorful tail and wing patches to startle insects into flight - they'll flash their bright patches to scare bugs out of hiding, then snatch them right out of the air with acrobatic precision.
confusionNotes: Female redstarts are often confused with other small, dull warblers, but no other New England warbler constantly fans and flicks its tail like a redstart. Remember: if it's acting like it can't sit still and keeps showing off its tail, it's probably a redstart regardless of color.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - American redstarts are completely unrelated to the European redstarts despite sharing the same common name. This is a classic example of early settlers naming New World birds after familiar Old World species that looked similar.
compareHints: Among the Setophaga warblers, American redstarts are unique for their hyperactive tail-fanning behavior and contrasting black-and-orange (or gray-and-yellow) pattern. Other warblers in this genus like Yellow-rumped or Pine Warblers have colorful patches but lack the redstart's constant motion and dramatic flashing displays. The restless, almost butterfly-like behavior combined with the flashing tail pattern makes redstarts unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the bright, all-yellow American Goldfinch, Yellow-rumped Warblers have more complex patterns and are smaller with thinner bills.

Among its Setophaga relatives, Yellow Warbler is the most uniformly yellow – Pine Warblers have white wing bars and are less bright, while Yellow-rumped Warblers only have yellow patches rather than being yellow all over.
Among the Setophaga warblers, Palm Warbler is unique for its ground-foraging behavior and constant tail-pumping.

Among its Setophaga cousins, the Black-throated Green is distinguished by its combination of yellow face and black throat - the Black-throated Blue lacks yellow entirely, while the Blackburnian Warbler has fiery orange instead of yellow.

Among its Setophaga warbler relatives, the Pine Warbler is notably less hyperactive than species like the American Redstart or Magnolia Warbler, and lacks the bold patterns of Black-throated Green or Chestnut-sided Warblers.

Among New England's Setophaga warblers, the Chestnut-sided is unique in combining white underparts with chestnut side markings - Bay-breasted Warblers have chestnut but also on the head and throat, while other common species like Yellow and Black-throated Green Warblers lack chestnut entirely.
Among the Setophaga warblers, Northern Parulas are unique for their blue-gray backs combined with yellow underparts - most other yellow warblers in this genus have olive or green backs instead.

Among its Setophaga warbler relatives, the male Black-throated Blue is unique for its solid blue upperparts and white belly combination - Black-throated Green Warblers have yellow faces and olive backs, while Northern Parulas have yellow throats and white wing bars.
Among the Setophaga warblers, Magnolia Warblers are unique with their combination of white wing patches (not just bars), yellow underparts with black streaking, and distinctive tail pattern.
Among New England's Setophaga warblers, breeding male Blackpolls are unique with their solid black caps and white cheeks - no other warbler in the region has this exact pattern.
Among its Setophaga relatives, the Blackburnian's orange throat is completely unique - no other warbler in this genus has anything close to that fiery coloration.

Among the yellow Setophaga warblers in New England, Prairie Warbler stands out with its bold black side streaks - Yellow Warblers lack these stripes entirely, while Pine Warblers have much fainter, less distinct markings.
Among the many Setophaga warblers, Cape May Warblers stand out with their unique curved bill and specialized nectar-feeding behavior that most of their relatives don't share.
Among its Setophaga relatives, the Bay-breasted Warbler is unique in having that rich chestnut breast coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Setophaga relatives, the Hooded Warbler is unique for its combination of a black hood (males) and white outer tail feathers that both sexes constantly flash.

Among its Setophaga warbler relatives, the Cerulean is unique for its pure blue and white coloring with the black chest band - most other warblers in this group are yellow-based (like Yellow Warbler) or have different patterns entirely (like the Black-throated Blue's dark throat and flanks).

Unlike its common cousin the Pine Warbler, which has a more olive-yellow throat and lacks bold face stripes, the Yellow-throated Warbler is much more dramatically marked with its bright golden throat and black mask.
Among its Setophaga relatives in New England, Townsend's Warbler is most similar to Black-throated Green Warbler but shows more extensive yellow coloring and bolder black face markings.
Unlike the Black-throated Green Warbler which has yellow on the face and olive upperparts, the Gray Warbler maintains its monochrome palette.
Among its Setophaga relatives in New England, Hermit Warbler is most similar to Black-throated Green Warbler but lacks the green tones entirely, showing gray instead.
